newsitem.title: PERU: Peru mediators meet rebels amid hints of progress.
newsitem.headline: Peru mediators meet rebels amid hints of progress.

text.p: Mediators met with Peruvian guerrillas holding 72 hostages to restart face-to-face talks with the government amid a few tenuous signs of progress in resolving the siege peacefully.

The three-man mediation panel known as the guarantors' commission met for two hours on Saturday with the rebels in the besieged home in Lima, where submachinegun-toting guerrillas have been holding hostages for 96 days.

Guarantor and Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani said later the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels gave renewed assurances that their captives -- a VIP list of cabinet ministers, ambassadors and businessman -- would not be harmed.

"We have received again from the MRTA a commitment to care for and treat respectfully all the hostages," Cipriani told reporters late on Saturday, joined by commission member and Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent.
But endless negotiations were not enough and now the commission wanted real steps to free the hostages, he said.
"Evidently, we want to see them free. We don't want just more conversations," he said.

There were signs the mediators were seeing results in efforts to steer talks away from the rebels' main demand of freedom for 450 jailed comrades -- a demand flatly rejected by President Alberto Fujimori -- and toward other issues.
First, Cipriani met for more than two hours with Cuban Ambassador Pedro Diaz, whose country along with the Dominican Republic has offered asylum to the hostage-takers if all sides agreed.

Cipriani said he was only bidding goodbye to the ambassador before he returned to Havana, but the meeting, joined by papal nuncio Fortunato Bardelli, inevitably led to speculation they were working out asylum details.

Red Cross doctors visited on Saturday a prison at a naval base in the port of Callao to check on the health and jail conditions of MRTA prisoners, diplomatic sources said. Top- ranking MRTA inmates are locked inside the tightly guarded seaside base -- including maximum leader Victor Polay.
The visit followed a visit on Friday by the same delegation to another prison housing MRTA women prisoners.
Improving prison conditions for the rebels was believed to be one of the main concessions Fujimori was willing to make to the MRTA, and the visits fuelled speculation about progress on that front.
The rebels blasted into a gala reception at the house on Dec. 17, 1996, and took the 500-some guests hostage, gradually releasing all but 72.
Fujimori flew on Saturday with the Japanese ambassador's wife to the Amazon lowland town of Pucallpa to distribute Japanese-donated blankets and clothes to flood victims.
It was the first public activity by the ambassador's wife since she and her husband were taken hostage. She, along with all the other female captives, were released in the siege's first hours.

At the besieged residence, tension was high following a leaked police report saying that well-armed MRTA rebels had slipped into Lima and were planning to carry out bomb attacks and possibly more takeovers.

Fujimori's chief negotiator tried to reassure the mediators and the Peruvian public he was ready to talk with the hostage- takers, after Cipriani chided both sides for letting negotiations languish while hostages suffered.
Negotiator Domingo Palermo also dismissed Cipriani's suggestion that the mediators might give up on the slow pace of talks and simply quit.

"We are ready and hoping that at any moment the talks can resume," said Palermo. "The guarantors have done an excellent job and I think they'll stay with it for a lot longer. They have great willpower, and they'll keep working until we find a solution, and so will we."
